speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion in the following case of urgent and pressing necessity. I refer to the situation that has developed in western Ontario, particularly along the Grand River, since the repeal of the Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act which provided federal and provincial assistance to municipalities wishing to carry out conservation projects so necessary for pollution control, projects which would assist municipalities faced with mounting unemployment and welfare costs.
Therefore, with consent, I intend to move that the Canada Water Act, 1970 be amended by the addition of a formula for assistance to municipalities similar to that incorporated in the Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act and that the House refer this matter to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works for consideration and report.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the last figures I have from the office of the Attorney General of Quebec as at 11.30 this morning are to this effect: 439 were arrested; 378 have been released; one was rearrested, and there are 62 detained. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may be allowed to answer the question directed to the Prime Minister, I have not to date been made aware by the provincial authorities of the details of any scheme of identification cards that they may have under consideration. maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE ON PROCLAMATION OF WAR MEASURES ACT
STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE ON PROCLAMATION OF WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister inform the House whether the Minister of Agriculture was expressing government policy on Thursday night in Manitoba when he said it would have been impossible for the government to produce documentary proof that the proclamation of the War Measures Act was necessary, and that the act was "too severe... unnecessary, under the circumstances..."?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE ON PROCLAMATION OF WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I myself admitted that the Act was too severe the very day I brought it into the House and I explained to the House that very shortly we were going to bring in another Act to replace it. However, under the circumstances even all opposition parties agreed there was a state of terror in Quebec at that time and that it needed exceptional measures which are not in the Criminal Code, and therefore this was the only way we could act with any expediency. I cannot vouch for what the minister said. He can do that for himself, but for that part of it, it is no great news. As I say, that was the government's position from the outset.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE ON PROCLAMATION OF WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister address himself to the first part of the question and indicate whether or not the government now believes it is not possible to prove it was necessary to bring in the Measures Act?

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE ON PROCLAMATION OF WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: It may be difficult to prove a negative, but it seems to me we now have the admission of all parties sitting opposite, in their very own words, that there was a state of terror in Quebec around the middle of October which needed extraordinary measures. There was some disagreement, I understand, about whether the Act was not too strong an extraordinary measure, but we conceded that from the outset. From the point of view of the need for extraordinary measures the opposition is conceding that even by voting for the new replacement legislation a full two weeks after the worst of the crisis is over. Therefore, retroactively, surely they must admit emergency measures were needed at that time.

maintopic: PRESENCE OF RUSTY BEETLE IN WHEAT SHIPMENTS- EFFORTS TO ELIMINATE

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORDERS
subsubtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some comments on this bill as we begin the detailed study of it clause by clause in committee of the whole. First of all, Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw to the attention of the committee the fact that we have had emergency situations in Canada before now. I say that as a member from the province of Saskatchewan where we had what was known in Canadian history as the Saskatchewan rebellion in 1885. That, of course, predates a good deal of the



November 9, 1970

modern history of the province of Saskatchewan and, indeed, of much of Canada. Nevertheless, that was a very important episode in the history of Canada in which a group of people who had a set of grievances against the government of Canada, and against many people in Canada, felt that they had to take strong action in order to try to rectify the situation. I think it would be fair to say that there are many people who today acknowledge that harsh and repressive steps were taken at that time. There were unnecessary steps taken at that time in dealing with the problems that existed. It must be acknowledged that some action must be taken when problems such as these arise. Nevertheless, unnecessary and harsh steps were taken. Unfortunately, some of the unhealthy effects, some part of the legacy of these steps, can still be seen in the pattern of events in Canada today, some 85 years later in our history.
I think this particular point can be best illustrated by some words that were uttered in Regina on October 2, 1968, on the occasion, I believe, of the unveiling of a statue in memory of Louis Riel who was hanged in 1855. The words of the statement are as follows:
How many other Hiels exist in Canada, beyond the fringe of accepted conduct driven to believe that this country offers no answer to their needs and no solution to their problems? How many of us understand the loneliness, the sense of futility of such a man? How many of us are willing to concede that future historians, in chronicling the events of our lives, may choose to emphasize and applaud the activities, not of the privileged majority but of some little-known leader of an unpopular minority?
For me this is the lesson of Louis Riel. For me this is the reason why we are here.
A democratic society and system of government, while among the grandest of human concepts, are among the most difficult to implement. In a democracy it is all too easy for the majority to forget the rights of the minority, and for a remote and powerful government to ignore its protests.
It is all too easy, should disturbances erupt, to crush them in the name of law and order. We must never forget that, in the long run, a democracy is judged by the way the majority treats the minority. Louis Riel's battle is not yet won.
Those word were uttered by the present Prime Minister in Regina on October 2, 1968.
This bill is extraordinary legislation and as such it imposes a special responsibility on legislators to examine both the general purposes and thrust of the bill as well as its specific contents very carefully. It imposes a special responsibility on the minister; this, I think, has to be said in view of the minister's credible record on many aspects of civil liberties.
Right now, I suggest, the minister's record is being put to the test. I hope that the minister will not take a rigid stand with respect to this bill. I hope that he does not even leave the impression that he has orders simply to hold the line with respect to this bill. I hope that he does not exhibit a non-flexible stand in dealing with the various proposals that will be put forward. The House has approved the principle that special legislation may be required to deal with situations such as this. We are prepared to consider the principle and to examine the bill based on that principle; but the contents and nature of the special powers contained in the bill still require
Public Order Act, 1970
close scrutiny. It does not necessarily follow that the particular provisions requested are justified merely by reason of the decision that special legislation is required. Thus, Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will be responsive to proposals made by the opposition. I think, if the minister is truly concerned about national unity, this concern will be reflected in a serious sensitivity to the many objections which have been registered both inside and outside the House about this legislation and about the previous actions of the government.
I certainly hope that we do not hear any more statements such as those the minister made on Wednesday last. I say this, Mr. Chairman, out of sadness and concern for what is happening rather than in anger. The minister first of all said that, certainly, it is the right of anyone to question the government's actions; but then he seemed to brand those who chose to question the government's actions. We even find that he accused those who were arguing against his stand of intellectual dishonesty. How can the minister take such a stand when he admitted in his remarks last Wednesday that the government's position represented a value judgment? Why is he so concerned about the fact that there has been opposition when he admitted that the government had taken harsh measures and when it was also admitted that not all of the facts have been made public? That is what the minister said on October 16. I suppose the minister had to defend himself, but I suggest he did himself no credit in his performance last Wednesday.
I think we are prepared to grant that the minister is human, as we all are. We hope, now that he has got this matter off his chest, he will be prepared to be both responsive and responsible. I do not have to remind the minister that not only is he responsible for carrying out the letter of the law and the letter of his duties as set out in the statute establishing his position and his department, but he has to ensure that justice is done, with all its implications and ratifications in Canada. I am sure it is not necessary to remind the minister of that.
[DOT] (3:10p.m.)
There are a number of serious questions which must be answered when considering this legislation. The first question I wish to ask the minister is whether there is still a need for this sort of legislation, taking into account the events as they have developed up to the present time. As expressed by their vote, some members approved of the action taken by the government and others disapproved. I am one of those who disapproved. However, that is now a matter of the past. We are looking at current events, the situation as it is today, and attempting to determine where we go from here.
In his remarks last Wednesday, the Minister of Justice indicated that there was still a continuing need for this sort of legislation. I accept that as an expression of his view, but the minister did not back up his statement with an adequate explanation of why he considers powers of this sort are still required. The minister owes this House such an explanation.

November 9, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
I wish to refer to what has occurred up to the present time. During this afternoon's question period the minister reported that 439 people had been arrested; that is approximately ten more than were reported last Thursday. Of these 439 people, 378 have been released; one has been rearrested and 62 are under detention at the present time. Charges have been laid against 40 of these 62 people. Last week the minister indicated that there were still approximately 40 people to be arrested. That is a small number.
The one reasonable point made by the government is-although I think there is an effective answer to the point-that the element of surprise was required when the government invoked the War Measures Act. However, that is now a matter of the past. The cat is out of the bag. The situation is being dealt with in the open. The government should be able to deal with most of the problems that remain through the provisions of the Criminal Code.
I suggest that hon. members have a responsibility to examine the implications of this bill and its consequences. Most members reluctantly conceded that there may be occasions when special powers are required, but I think most members would agree that special powers which infringe on the rights of people must be kept to an absolute minimum. We must demonstrate that our problems can and will be dealt with within the framework of responsible democratic government which safeguards human rights. If existing problems are responded to with repressive legislation, and it must be admitted there are repressive features in the bill now before us, that will reinforce the arguments of those against whom the government wishes to act and to whom we must answer in the long run in Canada's political development.
I wish to deal with a point raised on Friday by the hon. member for Calgary North. He recited an incident which occurred near his home in the early 1930's. A shooting occurred at a meeting being addressed by Mr. M. J. Coldwell. This resulted from the pressure created by discussion of the problems that existed in the 1930's. I have attended many of Mr. Coldwell's meetings, both as a boy and as an adult I have know him personally for most of my life. I can state that there is no more non-violent man in all of Canada. I do not wish to suggest that the member for Calgary North left a different impression, quite the contrary. However, it must be pointed out that men such as M. J. Coldwell, and the present leader of the New Democratic Party, succeeded in keeping hope alive in Saskatchewan and the rest of western Canada in the 1930's at a time when we were faced with difficulties as great or greater than those with which we are faced at the present time. That is important to note. These men kept alive the idea that things could be and would be better, and that changes and improvements could be brought about through the democratic process.
During the past week or two there have been many quotations from the book published, or about to be published, by Pierre Valliere, one of those arrested and against whom charges have been laid. He has been quoted in a number of newspapers. This man points out
the deplorable conditions under which he was raised. I can point to many examples I have witnessed of people who have been raised under conditions as bad or worse than those described by Mr. Valliere. The important point is that for many of those people who lived under such conditions, hope was kept alive that changes and improvements could be made. That is a critical point. I think most people will admit that hope has been snuffed out for some people in Canada today. Those with that feeling will be joining groups such as the FLQ. We must demonstrate our faith in the democratic process and show that it will work. By keeping repression to a minimum and by tackling the social and economic problems that exist, we will show that democracy does work.
There has been a good deal of discussion on various sections of the bill. I do not intend to repeat all of the comments which have been made. At the present time we are debating clause 2 of the bill which sets out the definitions. When we note the definitions in this legislation, we realize the far-reaching implications of the bill before us. A wide definition is given to such terms as "communicate", the group which may be classified as peace officers, statements, and unlawful association. I wish to deal briefly with one of the definitions. I hope the minister is listening from behind the curtain because this point must be dealt with. It is the definition of a peace officer.
The hon. member for Matane made some points with respect to this definition last Friday. I wish to raise one further point. The definition of a peace officer is extended beyond that provided in the Criminal Code to "include the members of the Canadian Forces". I am prepared to acknowledge that under emergency situations, when legislation such as this may be put into force, there may be a need to give members of the Canadian Forces the powers of a peace officer. However, as the subsection is worded at the present time, it is open-ended. It automatically gives a member of the Canadian Forces the power of a peace officer. This is my interpretation of the problem as a layman, although I have discussed the matter with other people. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that a safeguard needs to be placed in this particular extension of the definition of a peace officer by adding certain words in relation to members of the Canadian Forces. I suggest the following words might be added after the word "Forces"-"when assigned to perform the duties of a peace officer under the authority of a competent civil authority". I would be interested to hear the minister's comments on this proposal. When we are dealing with special legislation of the kind before us, I believe we must be doubly careful to see there is adequate legislative provision to ensure maintenance of civil authority over the military. I am not suggesting there is any present danger involving the situation or position of the Armed Forces, but we should not leave the door ajar when such an issue arises.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
One of the main thrusts of this bill is to be found in clause three which outlaws the FLQ. I think all of us would agree without argument that there are undesirable

November 9, 1970

aspects to the activities of the FLQ and that some action should be taken to deal with them. The question is, what kind of action is best suited to meet the circumstances. First of all, how wide a net does the government intend to cast upon the basis of its definition of FLQ or associated organizations? Is there a significant danger that innocent people will be caught in such a net when this bill comes into force? Second, there is the point which has already been discussed by various speakers in this debate, as well as on second reading, concerning the effectiveness in practice of any provision outlawing a particular organization. Is this really the way to get at the problem in the long run? Many people hold the view, that it is not.
There is also a curious circumstance which arises as a result of the termination date which has been inserted in the legislation. Clause 3, as I say, provides for the outlawing of the FLQ, but there is also included in the bill a termination date.

I thank the committee for its indulgence. I assure hon. members that I shall not take too long. As I was saying, provision is made for this legislation to terminate on April 30. After that date, presumably, the FLQ will no longer be an outlawed organization. The government has spoken about bringing in some form of permanent legislation. Is it intended that the FLQ shall continue to be outlawed after April 30? It seems to me we are faced, now, by a curious feature which requires further examination.
I further suggest that attention be paid to the wording of the preamble to the bill. The second paragraph contains a description of what it is about the FLQ that we do not like; as to a good many points contained in that description, there will be no argument, but I wonder whether this is sufficient background to establish the need for this legislation. Again, in the third paragraph of the preamble, reference is made to the invocation of the War Measures Act. It is, of course, true that this took place and that this particular step was approved by a vote in this House. Nevertheless, I question whether it is necessary to make this particular reference in such a way as to imply there was over-all approval of the action of the government up to this particular point in time. Possibly the wording should be reconsidered.
In conclusion, I submit that the amendments proposed by my hon. friend from Greenwood, and outlined by him on Friday, should be most carefully considered by the
Public Order Act, 1970
House if we are to handle this legislation in a responsible way. It involves our approach to the issues of civil disorder, of terrorism, to the extent it exists, and to the protection of citizens' rights throughout this country. The legislation before us has political and social consequences which go far beyond the impact of this particular measure. Each of us has a heavy responsibility. In my opinion, members of this House have dealt with this matter in a responsible way so far. The opposition has responded by its vote on second reading, a vote which indicated it was prepared to consider further a measure which provided special powers to deal with the situation which the Minister of Justice and others have described. It has been introduced on the basis of certain facts which are known, and others which have had to be deduced or assumed; we certainly need more explanation of this aspect. But I maintain the opposition has responded. It is now up to the government to respond, in turn, to the opposition's proposals. History will judge us on the basis of our sensitivity and adherence to democratic principles during this difficult time for Canada.

Across the country various radio stations, or at least their representatives, have been advised, informed, made aware, that the publication of certain material would not be in the public interest. Indeed, as far as certain universities are concerned, the student bodies who edit university papers have been given to understand that they are subject to censorship, and that censorship applies today despite the fact that the minister stated clearly, unequivocally and properly that legally it could not be applied.
This is the most dangerous form of censorship, the subtle kind that determines what I shall read, what I shall see, what I shall hear, without there being any legal justification for such censorship. The minister used these words-and I give him the opportunity of saying whether or not he actually used them. He said that there was no censorship of the news as far as radio or television stations and the like were concerned. Unless they were being used as propaganda agencies, he said, there would be no interference.
I should like to know who determines whether they are being used as propaganda agencies. Is not that the essence of censorship-that somebody determines for me what is propaganda and what is not propaganda? On this basis, certain ministers of the Crown should have kept their mouths shut, for some of the statements made by them indicate an irresponsibility that is not in keeping with membership on the government benches.

That is what I like about a debate in this House, Mr. Chairman, with opinions being exchanged. I am glad to have that statement from the minister, because accepting his view we have censorship in Canada. It is censorship not legally brought into effect, but rather left to certain individuals who determine whether a radio or T.V. station or the press itself comes within the definition of the words just enunciated by the minister. I suggest this is a dangerous proposition. It is of the essence of the imposition of censorship without accepting the responsibility of having censorship put into effect either by Parliament or, as under the wartime regulations, by order in council.
I pass on now to the next phase. For several days I have been trying to get some information regarding certain individuals who were alleged to be with Radio Canada-news broadcasters, commentators and the like. There were three or four of these people. This is not a matter picked out of the air; rather it comes from the confines of the mind of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. On many occasions he stated that several people were involved, and in every phase. One began to look at ministers of the Crown, even at parliamentary secretaries and Members of Parliament. He said that the dangerous permeation of this philosophy through the various strata of society had undermined everything. As a matter of fact, the minister used some very big figures. In Ottawa, the minister stated be thought the FLQ had 3,000 members. When the minister appeared on a television program with Jack Webster, he was reported to have said that the figure was twenty-five to fifty thousand. The minister spoke of thousands of weapons and masses of dynamite. Then he went on: "We can't tell you everything because if we did the security of the state would be undermined".
Then, the minister of Indian affairs joined in, and he drew a horrid picture of fear and danger. He said: "We can't tell you. We know, but if we were ever to tell it would bring into focus men high in public life, and we can't do that". This is all nonsense, Mr. Chairman. Like every member of the House, I have been following the evidence given at the inquest last Saturday in the city of Montreal. If you read the evidence given by the man Lortie, it is the most infantile example of amateurism that could have been put together. The government said that these were professional wrongdoers. In my view, if Lor-tie's evidence is accepted, their whole conduct indicates they were a bunch of novices.
To return to the people employed by Radio Canada, according to one minister, and by inference another, these people were actually engaged in using a code for the purpose of passing on information to FLQ members while pretending to be giving the news. They interpolated certain statements, observations or letters in one way or another into their reports. Three or four of these people were picked up, and that is what should have happened to them.
However, I have been trying to find out what has happened to these gentlemen. The Secretary of State has had several days to find out. Can you imagine the colos-

sal wisdom inherent in the statement that he made today? He said: How do we know who they were? How do we know which ones were released? I am not going to designate what I consider that statement to be, but I think that even the Minister of Justice will know what I have in mind.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
These people were traitors to this country. They operated within Radio Canada to undermine the state; to ensure that the FLQ conspirators would be successful in their aims. It must be taken that they were trying to cover up the tracks of those who kidnapped Mr. Cross and the minister of the Crown of the province of Quebec. They were passing out information and then they were picked up. Where are they now? The very fact that the minister, in the last few days, refused to give information in that connection would seem to indicate that they are back on the job. That is what we have been trying to find out. They are paid by the taxes of the people of Canada, and on the basis of a statement made by one of the ministers of the Crown in the present government, they were actually engaged, not only in a seditious operation but in something even close to treason itself.
They are picked up. They are taken into custody. They are released. Where are they now? I would like to know. Is the minister in a position to advise as to whether or not these people are back on the job? That is all I am trying to find out. I was surprised the ministers did not have some communication between themselves in that connection and ask, "These quadruplets of treason and treachery-where are they"? They were on the job with Radio Canada. They were engaged in nefarious and treacherous work. They were picked up. Where are they? Have they been released? It has been stated that they have been. Where are they now? If they are back in the CBC, the people of Canada as a whole will be able to conclude a great many things.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one who supported the implementation of the War Measures Act, I should like to speak on this clause. A number of weeks have passed and we have had an opportunity to look at the events and at the public evidence, some of the not so public evidence, and some of the inferences and circumstances surrounding the events of that time. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, I have no reason at this time to doubt or regret the decision I then took. I still feel it was correct to implement the War Measures Act and if I had it to do over again I would support it. Others, of course, had doubts to begin with and at least one member had reason to express his doubts just the other day. The decision concerning whether or not the introduction of the War Measures Act was correct will not be decided at this time. History will decide it or it may very well be that this debate will never be resolved because all the people involved obviously gave their actions a great deal of thought. They had to make decisions based on their judgment of the situation.
Today, however, the issue before us is whether the War Measures Act should be replaced with a more circumscribed measure and, on this occasion, I find I cannot support the government. I had hoped that some legislation could be introduced that would meet the needs of emergency situations but would not contain the dangerous provisions of the War Measures Act. I have looked at the bill before us. I have even looked at the amendments my party is offering to this bill as well as the amendments of the official opposition. Even if all these amendments were accepted, I do not think I could support the bill. I do not see how a bill could be drafted, containing some of the powers asked for, which could be considered safe or satisfactory. If we look at our Criminal Code, we will realize it has been developed over hundreds of years so we have been able to place certain safeguards in it. The minute you remove any of those safeguards you depart very sharply from the traditional concepts of freedom, which is an aspect of our society I like.
Therefore, any emergency legislation that departs from the present provisions and safeguards in the Criminal Code in my view is dangerous. This brings me to the point of view that the only time such emergency powers can be justified is during extreme conditions, and then only for a short period. I can see no justification for prolonging legislation of a dangerous nature beyond the immediate circumstances that call for the implementation of such legislation. In some ways, I believe the legislation before us is more dangerous than the War Measures Act.
I am not saying this from a legal point of view because I am not in a position to make that kind of a legal judgment. I do not have a legal background. I say this from the psychological point of view. Whatever the dangers may be of the War Measures Act, it has one advantage. This is an argument that was first advanced by the hon! member for Skeena. This legislation is so terrible in its
November 9, 1970

Implication, and so jeopardizes every one of our civil liberties, that its very danger is its safety. We know its dangers and what could happen if it should be prolonged. Since, we are aware of this-and the government obviously is aware of it-we are on our guard and are .careful about how it should be used.
Everytime someone starts talking about using the War Measures Act, whether in respect of hippies or school teachers, one becomes aware of the real concern of the members of this House. We realize how dangerous an instrument the War Measures Act is, and how careful we must be with it. Now, we have a bill before us which says, in effect, that the War Measures Act is too broad, too dangerous, and therefore we must bring in legislation which, to some extent, can deal with the problem in a more specific manner and remove the difficulties with which we are trying to deal. I am suggesting that once we take this attitude, once we think we can curtail civil liberties in a mild way, we are on the road to finding ourselves in serious difficulty. We are pretending this course is not dangerous. What is worse, there is an additional danger of isolating the problem to the province of Quebec and the FLQ because many people will say this legislation is better since it takes us off the hook and places on the hook those who should be there.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I am suggesting it is not possible to curtail the civil liberties of any group in this country without curtailing the civil liberties of everyone. I think whenever we see this kind of curtailment we must all continue to be on guard in respect of how it may affect us personally. It is a great mistake to try to isolate one group and pretend that the civil liberties of this country are not in danger. We just heard a very moving address by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert. He pointed out the difficulties that are already arising as a result of the implementation of the War Measures Act. We have had admissions from the Minister of Justice that people may have been picked up who were not guilty and who have been released. What does this mean? It means we are living with an enormously dangerous instrument and it is not possible to design an instrument that is in harmony with our traditional concept of liberty in this country. The only safeguard, if there is a safeguard, is, first, that we are constantly on guard against the implications of such emergency legislation and, second, that we remove it as quickly as the emergency disappears.
I want to suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that in my view the implementation of the War Measures Act did accomplish some useful objectives. If there was an apprehended insurrection-it does not appear to be the case now-in some respects we have achieved a short term gain. However, there are many things that we have not accomplished. We had hoped to save the life of Pierre Laporte. The War Measures Act was not able to do this, and neither will this legislation. We may still be able to save the life of Mr. Cross, and all of us are hopeful that this win be possible. If the War Measures Act will in any way contribute toward this objective, then it will be helpful.
Public Order Act, 1970
It seems to me that the chief advantage of the implementation of the War Measures Act is that we have, in some ways, won a psychological victory. For years now, people in Canada have been very concerned about violence in our society. This violence is not limited to Quebec. People have been concerned about violence in the world, violence in North America, and they have been worried that the government would be unable to cope with it. Now, I think they have to be told that violence has deeper causes than can be cured by legislation alone. But they have to be reassured that, to the extent that legislation is helpful or can be useful, the Parliament of Canada has that legislation at hand and is prepared to use it on their behalf. It seems to me that this is an important thing to say to the people of Canada. We must say to them "Don't be frightened; don't panic, Parliament can and will act if it is necessary". We have made that point.
Whether or not this bill passes, the War Measures Act will still exist. The Parliament of Canada can invoke it in an emergency if it is required. It seems to me that we will lose that short term psychological victory if we continue this or any subsequent act beyond the period of the immediate emergency. At any rate, there can be no justification now for continuing emergency legislation, let alone for contemplating writing a new piece of legislation. Rather than look back or hang on to something which in my view has done some good, we now have to direct our attention to the long term problems associated with violence in our society. Unless we do that, and unless we act quickly, we can lose the advantage we gained through the implementation of the War Measures Act.
What are those things about which we should be thinking? I do not believe legislation is the answer. It is useful up to a point, but it will not solve the problem. Although there are people who objected to the position that my leader took when he talked about the underlying root causes, the economic problems of Quebec-there are people who say that the revolutionaries are middle class, they are not poor-let there be no mistake that this is where the problem really lies. It may be that we could solve the economic problems of Quebec, and Quebec might still wish to separate. It may be that we could solve these economic problems, and there might still be violence. But let us be sure about one thing, there is a chance of success in this course. The other course, that is the use of emergency legislation, offers no chance of success. Either we solve the deep rooted problems, many of them economic, many of them social, that afflict the people of Quebec, that are real grievances in the minds of people who are not revolutionaries or fanatics, who are not terrorists, or we will have gained nothing. The turmoil and soul searching that this House has been through will have been for no purpose at all.
I think there are dangers if we continue with emergency legislation. We are going to create a whole new set of martyrs. I cannot see how you can have legislation that asserts guilt by association and say it is fair legislation or that it is an improvement over the War Measures Act. This is just not possible. Even if you remove the retroac-
November 9, 1970

Public Order Act, 1970
tive features of the legislation, which I think would probably make the whole bill pointless, you would still be left with legislation that is not fair. The minute you say that membership per se, or the support of any organization per se, constitutes a crime, you violate one of the basic premises on which our freedom is based. I do not think I have to demonstrate this. I am quite prepared to be tough in defence of democracy. I think that the defenders of democracy can make a mistake by being excessively permissive, but I think they are also wrong if they are tough and unfair for no good purpose.
Therefore, I think it would be a mistake for us to use the War Measures Act to charge those who are now held, and thus to create a set of martyrs. The longer they are kept in prison, the greater will be their martyrdom. Sooner or later, they will have to be let out, and sooner or later the memory of the atrocious murder of Pierre Laporte will recede from people's minds; their grievances will come to the forefront. People will forget the terrible violence and remember only their present unhappiness. This is a danger. One only has to look at the history of violence in other countries to see that many of the leaders came to their positions as a result of the martydom of imprisonment. It is difficult to think of these people as martyrs, but it is even more difficult to think of them as leaders now. However, let us learn something from the past.
There is also the danger that if we prolong this measure beyond the immediate and specific emergency, we will discredit the ability of the democratic system to operate at all. For instance, when will this legislation be withdrawn? It is becoming a crutch. The legislation will be in effect until April of next year. Is the FLQ going to go away by April? Are the difficulties in Quebec going to disappear by April? Will violence stop in Canada, in North America, in the world, by April? I do not think so. Whenever you try to withdraw this legislation, there may be some event, a death, a kidnapping, a bombing, that will prevent its withdrawal, and people will learn to live with this legislation. They will learn to justify the injustices. They will learn to forget about those who have been in prison and released, and will learn to accept this as a measure which had to be adopted, although it was unfortunate. It will become a great crutch. The police will say "we cannot operate without it". It will become more and more difficult rather than less and less difficult to remove this legislation as time goes on. Let us do it now.
To a very large extent, the House of Commons has shown its willingness to be the conscience of the nation, as some members decided to be; to be tough, as other members decided to be, but it has acted. No member in the House has stood in the way of Parliament acting decisively. Therefore, I think we could take this opportunity to withdraw this bill and withdraw the War Measures Act along with it.
The other danger is that we are going to drive the FLQ underground. The minister will probably say they are underground anyway. It is true that murderous activities are always underground, but we can deal with them
through the Criminal Code. Most criminal activity that can be dealt with by the Criminal Code is underground. But let us look at the situation. Who has been picked up? The people who were underground were not picked up, but the people who were above ground, who spoke publicly and who could be identified. If you drive the FLQ underground, then you will not know who to pick up the next time; you will have to do everything in the dark.

They have also proven they can be tough in defence of democracy. The public has been reassured by this act, and Parliament has shown that it can move quickly. Now is the time to withdraw that act, and now is the time to stop thinking of short term legal approaches. We should commit ourselves to an honest attempt at solving the long term and significant problems of the province of Quebec because those are the problems which create conditions on which violence feeds.

One of the greatest disservices of this government was that, instead of attempting to quiet down the substantial emotions in this country during this period, it has in fact done exactly the reverse. I find it odd that the Prime Minister never questioned the reason why hon. members from Quebec on both sides of the chamber so willingly voted in support of the steps being taken. His interpretation is that what he is doing is absolutely right. That is his privilege. Looking a little deeper, I suggest that the unanimity on the part of the Quebec members was an indication of the tremendous sense of fear, indeed the word fear is too weak to indicate the panic that existed amongst the people of the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec during the past few weeks.
It could be argued that by adopting these sweeping measures the government has, in effect, restored the loss of public morale. That may be true on the short term, but I fear for the long term. One can only reflect on the extent to which it would be very easy, if indeed acts of terrorism were to recur in one month, three months or three years, for the people of Montreal and the province of Quebec to have a much better understanding of the problem, if they could see that root causes of terror were being removed. The response of massive police and military intervention is immediate and effective, but it carries with it great dangers. Its successful termination of the problem may be shallow.
We must recognize that there has been a substantial body of opinion in the province of Quebec that has been increasingly alienated, not only from the federal system of government which we have in this country, but from the total operation of government. We must not accept that kind of feeling passively or simply react with hostility. We must try to understand and resolve those frustrations in the best interests of the country, not by

Public Order Act, 1970
appealing to the worst instincts of men, violence, prejudice and hatred, but by appealing to their best instincts, idealism, humanitarianism and participation. If we do that, we will have no just cause to fear. If we place our inner and physical security on repressive legislation, we will do little to deal with the root cause of violence which is what this debate is all about.
How are we going to deal with the problem of violence? Through invoking the War Measures Act regulations and by introducing this bill, the government has indicated that these are the necessary laws to deal with violence. By reading this bill and the War Measures Act regulations, I, not being a lawyer, find that they state what is to be done after the violence has occurred. Are we incapable of responding in some fashion and only able to deal with situations of such proportionate violence after they have occurred? We must address ourselves to the causes and prevention of violence in our country. That is our basic responsibility. If we do not do that, it may appear by the repressive measures that we are taking, and the publicity included in the process, that we are giving some aura of attractiveness and even martyrdom to those who least deserve it. Not only must justice be done, but it must appear to be done so that violence will not occur in our society.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert described one process that would balance the tremendous powers the government feels are necessary with the responsibility it has to the people of this country. The government is again hoping to have these powers accepted through this temporary public order bill. If the government, in good conscience, feels such legislation is necessary, it has a duty to provide some kind of balance to these sweeping powers. We have heard about the possibility of parliamentary committees. Indications are there will be amendments suggesting judicial commissions.
Shortly following World War II there was a national crisis in this country. The then Prime Minister came into possession of a network of intelligence that was being communicated to a foreign nation. There was the great danger that there had developed a very elaborate spy system in this country. At that time the Prime Minister decided to take extraordinary powers to arrest and detain certain individuals. He also appointed the Tas-chereau and Kellock Commission, which reported to Parliament on an interim basis, and on the termination of the commission made a final report. I am speaking of course about the Gouzenko affair.
The Gouzenko affair was not exactly parallel to the present situation, but it was a national crisis. It was recognized that the government required special and sweeping powers. The Liberal government of that day felt that it was not sufficient to simply say, "We know what is best. We have the facts, but the need for these powers will be difficult to prove; just give us the powers." They said: We shall take these powers but we shall ensure the public welfare by setting up an independent judicial commission which will report to Parliament. It must surely seem reasonable to members of this committee, and to citizens of this country as a whole, that any

government which seeks such powers as have been exercised for the past three weeks should also be ready to commit itself to a role of public stewardship, and the only means by which I see this being done is the establishment of a judicial commission of the kind suggested. I wonder whether the government of the day can really believe it is exercising a public trust unless it accepts this kind of discipline and this kind of stewardship on behalf of the people.

Mr. Chairman, regarding clause 2, I would have three remarks.
First, concerning clause 2 (d), one might, at first sight, find it purposeless. As a matter of fact, it is not so, for its main purpose, I think, is to make an equivalence in English between "the unlawful association" and "an unlawful association", and in French between "l'associa-tion illegale" and "une association illegale". I feel this is deplorable. Indeed, it is because of this clause 2 (d) that, in the remainder of the bill, there will be no further reference to "an unlawful association" but only to "the unlawful association". In other words, this clause is used to conceal, psychologically so to speak, the fact that this bill not only affects the FLQ, as stated earlier, even in the preamble, but also other associations.
Clause 4 says that it is prohibited to be a member of the unlawful association. Well, under clause 2 (d), it should be "an unlawful association", and I will show that in clause 3, it cannot be defined. In fact, each time the expression, "the unlawful association" appears in the bill, it should read instead, "an unlawful association".
Accordingly, I suggest first that clause 2 (d) be simply removed.
My second comment has to do with the logical sequence in the wording of the bill. Clause 2 is entitled, "Interpretation", and it defines some words. Then, I do not see why clause 3 could not be included in clause 2 where phrases such as "communicate", "peace officer", "statements" and "the unlawful association" are defined. I think that clause 3, which gives a definition of "unlawful association" should replace the present clause 2 (d).
I propose to introduce the following change, which is only editorial and does not alter the substance of the wording:
"Unlawful association" means the group of persons or association known as the Front de Liberation du Quebec, any successor group or successor association thereof, as well as any group or association that advocates the use or force or crime to accomplish or as an aid in accomplishing the same or substantially the same governmental change within Canada as that advocated by the said Front de Liberation du Quebec.
Again, I propose to substitute the wording of clause 3 to clause 2 (d) and later on I will deal with the substance of clause 3.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, here is my most important comment which refers to clause 2 (b). When you look closely for the purpose of this act, you notice that obviously it is

not to decree heavier sentences. As a matter of fact, sections 60 and 62 of the Criminal Code stipulate that a person who advocates, without using it, the use of force to overthrow the government is liable to 14 years imprisonment, while under the present bill, the person who not only advocates, as stated in the Criminal Code, but effectively engages in the use of force, as stated in clause 4, (g), is liable to imprisonment of only five years.

That is the main thing, and I admit it with humbleness and vigour, so true is it that all Canadians agree to punish those who are guilty of the worst crime of all, to threaten this freedom of ours.

(b)	a warden, deputy warden, instructor, keeper, gaoler, guard and any other officer or permanent employee of a prison.
(c)	a police officer, police constable, bailiff, constable or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace or for the service or execution of civil process;
Many of these people do not come under police authority at all, and, in this specific instance, under the Quebec Police Act. The implication is that those many individuals will be empowered to make arrests on grounds of mere suspicion under clause 9(1) and keep people in jail up to seven days, or up to three days without the consent of the Attorney General who, evidently, cannot personally study each prisoner's file.
All the classes of persons I have just enumerated are peace officers, as defined in clause 2. They will be empowered, under clause 9(1), to arrest people because of mere suspicion and this without being liable to any suits for damages. The fact that arrest per se is a denial of justice is borne out by the Criminal Code's stipulation that arrest without warrant cannot be resorted to in the field of what are called, in our jargon, "criminal offenses". As a matter of fact, it can be used only if a person is caught red handed. Then, to arrest without warrant, the police must see the person really committing the offence. Only in the matter of crimes, he may arrest without warrant if he has reasonable and probable grounds, according to Section 435 of the Criminal Code.
Now, I suggest that precisely because it is a law of exception, this power should not be granted to an officer
Public Order Act, 1970
of the peace, under subclause (1) of clause 9, that is the power to make an arrest without warrant merely on suspicion. Too many people fall in this category.
Here is an example out of a thousand: The mayor of a small municipality is suspecting three bearded men who have just arrived. He will be able to put them under arrest merely on this suspicion.
Here is another example: During a municipal election campaign, the mayor suspects that his opponent wants to use "telegraphers", according to the familiar term, meaning impersonators on election day. He could then under such suspicion and without any recourse, under clause 9(1) and under one subclause in clause 4, subclause (g) in particular, arrest and detain his opponent during the last three days of the campaign.
Thus, honest people cannot help thinking that Dr. Bel-lemarre's arrest at the last municipal elections in Montreal was motivated by such considerations.
I therefore conclude as follows. I move that clause 2(b) be rewritten so as to limit this power of arrest without warrant-which is one of the main points of this legislation-to the limited classes of persons specified in the orders in council of the Governor General or of a Lieutenant Governor in council.
Finally, I remind the House that peace officers who for weeks have prevented some prisoners from seeing their lawyers-a right which is recognized in the Canadian Bill of Rights and which is not abrogated by the invocation of the War Measures Act-may have violated sections 408 and 107 of the Criminal Code.
In short, I wish to propose three amendments. First, subclause (d) should be struck out. In my view, it changes the whole aspect of this bill in which the words "unlawful association" are often repeated. Under that subclause those words cannot be used. Second, there is no logical order in the bill. In clause 2, "unlawful association" should be defined. Third, I propose that the definition of "peace officer" in subclause (b) of clause 2 be restricted to a category of persons, the list of which to be proclaimed by an order of the governor in council or the lieutenant-governors in council.
This is all I have to say about clause 2, Mr. Chairman.

I know that many members of the House would like to participate in this debate. I know a number of hon. members opposite, including the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), are very anxious to participate in it. I know it is a subject upon which we are all in agreement. I know they are just as anxious as I am to have the government bring down legislation to protect the consumer.

The Minister of Justice, in a very interesting paper which I am sure all hon. members have read, delivered at a seminar at Queen's University in May of this year, said:
The erosion of privacy is the beginning of the end of freedom.
He also said in the same paper:
The orbit of privacy will be an ever-shrinking one, but the need for privacy will become more paramount than ever. The law must ensure that the right to privacy remains sacrosanct.
I believe that this is a very serious matter. I think that 1984 is almost here. In this age of computers and data banks the citizens of Canada have no protection against false and misleading information which is often fed into computer banks and data processing centres-

I am sure that the hon. member, who is so anxious to interrupt me, has never had this problem because he was brought into this world with a silver spoon in his mouth and he doesn't know what we are talking about. But, if he does, perhaps he will favour us with a contribution to the debate before the hour is over.
There is a growing concern in this country over the question of the invasion of privacy, particularly with regard to commercial reporting agencies which gather information from peoples neighbours and friends, and sometimes from competitors, in order to report on individuals to credit card plans, to industries, to retailers, to banks, and in many cases to government agencies. When I think of the information, stored by computers of all sorts, on personal matters I just wonder whether the government or the private sector is going to win the race to 1984, which I believe is almost here.
Credit Records
I can accept the existence, indeed the need, for these reporting agencies. I believe that in many instances they perform a very useful and necessary function in helping to facilitate the business and commerce of the country, and in helping to avoid bad debts. However, what I object to is the fact that these agencies are allowed to function in a completely unregulated fashion. The time has come when we should give consideration to bringing in legislation which would make it necessary for these reporting agencies to apply for federal licences and to operate under the terms of those licences.
I know that hon. members will agree that this is an area of growing concern. It is one we read a great deal about. Indeed, many of us are becoming growingly concerned over the widespread use of computers and the techniques that are being developed to assimilate information about every single one of us, and about our private acts. While individuals may have partial rights to checking the information in these information banks, as legislators it is incumbent on us to ensure that the individual has complete rights in this particular regard. Most Canadians frequently voice a claim to the right to privacy as a basic right in our society. If we were to ask for 20 definitions of what we understood by that right to privacy perhaps we might come up with 20 different definitions. However, I am sure we would all be in agreement on one thing, the right of the individual to have his reputation protected from unscrupulous credit reporting, reporting against which he has no redress.
It is an awesome thing to consider that in this computer age with techniques so sophisticated that computers can store every minute detail of every piece of information. Already in California, a new model laser has been developed which is capable of providing 645 million items of data on a single square inch of magnetic tape. This means that this technique could efficiently store data in respect of every single citizen of Canada. Robert Merton, in his book "Social Theory and Social Structure" said:
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Privacy is not merely a personal predilection; it is an important functional requirement for the effective operation of social structure. Social systems must provide for a portion of the self which is kept apart, immune from social surveillance.
We must act now, I believe, to protect the individual whose rights and whose reputation could and, in many instances, often are taken away by false and misleading information without the individual concerned having any redress whatsoever. When we consider the enormity of this at a time when we are approaching what has been termed a cashless society, a society of credit cards, data information and computerized systems, then obviously the need exists for action to be taken soon.
I know hon. members will raise the question of jurisdiction. I know some hon. members who are very anxious to participate in this debate, and who are anxious to see the resolution brought to a conclusion by having a vote on it, will raise the problem of jurisdiction and the constitutional limitations placed upon Parliament. I would point out, however, that the Parliament of Canada has already acted in many

November 9, 1970
Credit Records
areas by bringing in legislation which requires consumer protection from unjust, false credit reports. For example, the Small Loans Act, the Bank Act, and indeed some provisions of the Income Tax Act come to mind. But apart altogether from these specific areas in which the government already has acted in a legislative way, recognizing the rights of the provinces in the area of proposed changes, what rights do I as a Canadian living in the province of Newfoundland enjoy if that province has no legislation in respect of credit agencies. In the province of Ontario there may be such legislation or, if not, it certainly is contemplated. But I would not enjoy the protection of the Ontario legislation if I did not live in that province.
For this reason, I believe as a federal Parliament we have a responsibility to act in this particular area. I believe there are many and ample constitutional precedents for doing so. Mr. Speaker, I know hon. members are becoming impatient to make their contribution. Before I conclude, however, I should like to refer hon. members to recommendation No. 18 of the Special Joint Committee on Consumer Credit. This committee did not make many very specific recommendations, but one specific recommendation it made concerned the setting up of a federal-provincial committee on consumer credit. Here, surely, the need for such a committee is manifest because the federal government must take the responsibility of protecting Canadians from being victimized by these computer banks, these data processing agencies and credit agencies, which go around collecting this information and selling it in many cases to the highest bidder. In many cases these agencies destroy the reputations of individuals involved without their ever having had any knowledge of it. Mr. Speaker, I commend this motion to members of the House. I ask that they support it and allow it to come to a vote.

Mr. Speaker, I am interested in proceeding, but I question the value of bringing in a lot of words which would look great in print, and probably help win a few votes, but which would do little to alleviate the situation until technology has advanced sufficiently to take care of these breaches of which my hon. friend complains. I have not heard any evidence from my learned friend concerning a number of flagrant breaches or abuses of these credit reports. There does not seem to be any mass outcry from anyone. I do not know whether my friend has received letters of complaint from Canadian citizens. I have had none, and I have heard of none having been received by members either on my side of the House or on his side of the House.
With great respect, may I say that I think the hon. member is really drumming up an issue which does not exist as an enforceable matter. We could pass regulations and make long impassioned speeches about the right to privacy which is not inscribed in any textbook on common law or in any statute. What is the right to privacy? There are the offences under trespass, assault, libel or slander. I really submit the law on libel and slander is probably the most efficient law by which to approach these wrongs. If it is possible to trace the person who maliciously or unfairly promoted an improper credit rating, there is action in the courts. The courts will find the damages. I say, leave it to a jury. A jury is composed of men who are very fair in sizing up the parties and in considering the merits of a situation. The jury would give consideration to the specific type of abuse to which my friend refers.
I suggest that basically the subject matter would be found to come within the purview of civil rights rather than credit and security regulations and, therefore, would come under the law of libel or slander rather than under any special legislation on credit which would normally come within the provincial sphere. If the House should find that the matter should be referred to a committee for consideration, I suggest that it be dealt with not in isolation but in the broader context of abuses by way of eavesdropping, wiretapping and the other so-called breaches of privacy, upon which I think legislation is needed.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The individual needs to have protection from abuses of this type, and the whole trend of our modern living is an attempt to catch up with the tremendous technological advances made by science. We have computers and we are worried in Canada today about whether we have control over our sources of information as a result of foreign computer industries entering the country. We
November 9, 1970

have to look at these problems in the context of a changing society, the post industrial era.
I submit that my hon. friend's motion has a lot of merit because it stimulates thought. I do not criticize him for it at all. I think it is great that we have this kind of discussion and research, and we should plod on with it. However, I would rather have seen some constructive ideas advanced regarding how he would propose to enforce the regulations. Does he envisage a sort of control board of counter-detective agencies or counter-electronic devices checking on officials? We might end up in a quagmire of electronic spying wars. This may be what it will come to, but I hope it never does. I hope that our teaching process will somehow develop the kind of Canadian most of us know, the kind of person who does not believe in snooping and backhanded methods. We will get there eventually, but we are certainly a long way from being able to control this situation.
My hon. friend did not specify what committee would deal with this matter if it ever gets to a committee. The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs dealt with the problem of wire tapping and eavesdropping. In spite of having had the Bell Telephone Company before it, and having had a demonstration of the type of electronic eavesdropping devices and wire tapping devices that are used, no conclusive legislation has been advanced to date.
We are hoping that the government, with the research staff it has available and, I hope, with its friendly relationship with the computer industry, will be able to find some practical answers. But then, we still have the unanswered question of enforcement. Will this be left in the hands of the police force or will it be left to the Attorney General? There are advantages one way and the other.
If my hon. friend's motion were to succeed, what department of government would undertake the administration of this measure? What sort of tribunal would be set up to enforce it? What sort of administrative group would work under the agency? What sort of cost would be involved? I submit that you would perhaps inhibit the value of having any creditable reports, and you would end up with an expense that would be positive but a result that would be negative. For those reasons, I am opposing the motion.

I am surprised that the hon. member for St. John's East did not present this motion in bill form. I find the motion to be extremely restrictive. It provides that the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to protect the privacy of every person against the improper disclosure of credit rating records and to protect the reputation of every person against any misinformation contained in such records. First of all, there is no suggestion by the hon. member for St. John's East that a person cannot be investigated without his knowledge, and it appears to me that this is where a great deal of the evil arises out of records of this nature. When a person is investigated without his knowl-

November 9, 1970

edge, hearsay evidence creeps into such a report, he is never presented with a copy of it, and for reasons never made known to him his contractual ability is affected. I think that, per se, is grossly unfair.
More and more we are coming to consider the protection of the privacy of the individual, making it the subject matter of modern legislation. More and more we are aware of the fantastic and overwhelming power of not only government but of bodies corporate acting in the commercial field within our society. Certainly, last year in the Justice Committee we spent a great deal of time on the invasion of privacy by electronic devices. Many provincial governments have passed legislation dealing with the subject. It is interesting to note from the Speech from the Throne that we can anticipate legislation along that line from this government.
In conjunction with this matter I would like to consider the problems pertaining to the storage of information about the person, the ability of machines to consolidate tremendous amounts of information about one person or many persons and to make it readily available throughout the world. Control of these machines and the organizations behind them must be a matter of great concern. One frightful aspect of this which is in the minds of us all is that of "Big Brother". As George Orwell wrote in "1984", the concept of government completely overshadows the privacy and right of the individual. The prospect of international corporations and multiconglomerate corporations having access to these data banks and the like which could so affect the individual in his daily life, is rather frightening. I think it is something with which we are concerned now and must be concerned about in the future.
As I have suggested, this resolution is relatively narrow in that it deals only with a very minor problem in relation to the whole issue. I have doubts about several aspects of the resolution. First of all, it has been suggested that it is a question that should properly be put in the hands of the federal government from a constitutional point of view. Certainly, it might be said to come within banks and banking, but it would not affect the many financial institutions which are subject only to the laws of the provinces in which they operate. Nor would it affect protective agencies which are under the law of the provinces and which so often find the information about which the hon. member complains.
It is certainly questionable whether it applies to the criminal law, though it is probably closer to that than any other aspect of the powers of the government of Canada. In that respect I am inclined to the view that it is far closer to provincial powers than to the Constitution. For my part, I am inclined to suggest that a resolution of this nature be left with the provincial government. In any event, the revelation of the material contemplated in the resolution might well be libellous and actionable if the motives of the person releasing it were not bona fide under the circumstances. I think it would be improper, under certain circumstances, to release such information even if it were the truth.
Credit Records
There are many circumstances which arise whereupon the disclosure of such information is very valuable to citizens of the community. For instance, somebody in the ordinary process of collecting judgment in the courts who wished to examine the ability of a judgment debtor to pay, would find this information of value, and surely it should be made available to the judgment creditor. I can think of many other situations that might arise which would limit this resolution in its present context.

Mr. Speaker, I too have sympathy for the hon. member's notice of motion and I commend him for bringing it forward. It is not too often that I disagree with the conclusions of the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Gibson), but in this instance I am at odds with some of them. That is one of the great things about being Liberals; we are not afraid to disagree among ourselves.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) might have said more on this motion instead of attacking an hon. member of this House. I suppose that since he is a member of one of the smaller opposition parties in the House, he and his group are seldom subject to criticism. As a result, they have become unduly sensitive. That has been demonstrated by the leadership contest, so called, that has taken place and powder puff fights that have taken place among leaders of that party.
The hon. member who introduced the notice of motion has not suggested that it is the be-all and end-all of this matter. I think he was probably right in not introducing a bill and in bringing this matter forward in the form of notice of motion. For the first time I have heard that hon. member admit that he does not have all the answers. That is quite right. I think he suggested that the problems raised by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth ought to be given careful scrutiny, and that they should be embodied in a government bill.
I have found, in talking to former clients of mine, that many of them have experienced difficulty in establishing a good credit rating or any credit rating. They see nothing wrong with someone inquiring about their credit background and very often say to the inquirer, "Go and speak to my bank manager." Often they mention someone with whom they have done business.
The notice of motion we are considering is carefully worded. The hon. member suggests that the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to protect the privacy of every person against the improper disclosure of credit rating records. That is the part that appeals to me. Very often an individual with a poor credit rating is unaware of his rating. Very often his poor credit rating results from an incident that took place when he was a young man and new in business. Perhaps then he was unable to pay a bill. That incident shows up on his credit rating and he may be unaware of it.

November 9, 1970
Credit Records
The invidious aspect of this is that he has no opportunity to defend himself when applying for credit. The bank may say to him, "We are sorry but we cannot grant you credit," and the applicant is not in a position to defend his record. Then the applicant begins to wonder if the debt he could not pay some years ago has more weight than he suspected on his credit record. He may wonder what the reason is for his poor credit rating. Nevertheless, the information is not made available to him; it is given only to the individual seeking information about his credit rating.
Often, when clients come to me and say, "Apparently I have a bad credit rating," the first thing I say is, "Do you deserve a poor credit rating? Do you have debts?" On the other hand, a person may early in his career have been sued, and as soon as action is instituted against the man, the credit bureau immediately takes cognizance of the fact. What the man's credit record does not show is whether he had a good defence to the action. If he is sued for a debt, that fact automatically is included in his credit record. What is not indicated, very often, is how the matter was resolved before the courts. Very often a person applying for credit may feel that he had a bona fide defence to the court action.
There are many instances in which an individual has been asked to defend an action wherein he is sued in respect of goods he has bought on credit. He may have bought the goods and signed a promissory note, and on refusing to pay on the promissory note because the goods were defective or not delivered, he is sued. The court will say to him that his defence is not a good defence in view of the promissory note; that his claim or counterclaim must be directed against the establishment which sold him the goods, but so far as the promissory note is concerned he owes the money and must pay.
Sometimes an individual in that situation will thumb his nose at his creditors, or perhaps leave the community. I remember one such incident. The individual returned two years later. The finance company sued him. By way of defence we alleged that the kind of interest the finance company was trying to collect was unconscionable. We were successful in our defence against the interest claim of the finance company. All too often such companies claim an usurious amount of interest on debt.
Another situation in which an individual is named as a defendant in a court action arises in the following manner. A person has bought a home, placed a first mortgage on the home and has paid regularly, say for five, six or seven years, on that mortgage. Then he has sold the house. The individual who has bought the house from him has made regular payments for a considerable time, then he has suddenly gone into default, possibly because of unemployment or other reasons. He has not kept up the payments. In that case the mortgagor sues, not only the individual who presently owns the home and who is responsible for making the payments but also the first owner because the name of the first owner is on the convenant under the terms of the mortgage. That person,
of course, has a perfectly good defence; he has paid his money. Surely, therefore, his credit rating should not suffer.
Because an individual has no opportunity to defend his credit rating, because he has no way of knowing whether he deserves his rating or not, I support the motion of the hon. member. It is not complete in its proposals. The hon. member does not say it is. It lacks many, many things. The hon. member is only suggesting that, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing-here I would add the adjective "appropriate"-legislation to protect the privacy of every person against the improper disclosure of credit rating records. Therefore, I support the motion of the hon. member, Mr. Speaker.
