Mr. Speaker, I should like first to commend the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) for introducing this motion which I think is quite necessary.
The hon. member is not the first one to object to the disclosure of facts concerning the private life of individuals. I remember reading, a few years ago, a book written by an American, Vance Packard, entitled Naked Society, where the activities of American credit bureaux were described in detail and which contained several cases where the life of an individual had been publicly revealed and scrutinized by those agencies.
Personally, for the last four years I have been closly associated with a large insurance company. I have had the opportunity to look at credit reports and I have often noticed, with disgust, that some of those credit reports contained information which had nothing to do with the financial situation of the persons involved. I read, in those credit reports, sentences such as these: "This individual is often intoxicated. He is a shady character and goes with several women."
I would say that those famous little pink reports often contain similar information and that they are handed to dealers, or any person who is in business and who regularly requests information of this kind from the credit bureau, information which have absolutely nothing to do with the financial situation, the steadiness and solvency of the individual involved.
Those are the reasons why I think the member for St. John's East is quite right in presenting his motion and I will support it.
I would like to offer two constructive solutions along this line, mainly intended for the Minister of Consumers and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) whom I invite to introduce soon in the House a piece of legislation aimed at protecting individual privacy.
This legislation should at least have two characteristics. First, a copy of any credit record should be sent to the individual concerned. I see no reason why a bill should not be submitted to the House including such a

November 9, 1970

provision and ensuring that the individual who has been inquired upon be sent a copy of the report. If this report is true, what is wrong with letting the individual involved having a copy of it? The individual is supposed to know the content of the report. Why not let him know the content of a report that will be circulated on request to several financial organizations?
And now my second recommendation: the individual receiving a copy of his report should be entitled to request the deletion of erroneous information contained in it.
I myself have checked the contents of certain reports with the people concerned. They contain, for unknown reasons, information that is entirely false, that was collected by the agent entrusted with the inquiry who could question neighbours, the neighbourhood grocer on the habits of the person concerned. Still, that information is in the report and often gives a distorted picture of the life of the individual.
To my mind, when we deal with facts and not opinions, and the facts are erroneous, on receiving copy of such a report, the individual should be able to have the false information deleted.
I feel, it might be well to introduce a bill containing far more details than those I have just mentioned. Such a bill would surely please the hon. member for St. John's East as much as me.
In closing, I merely wish to add that I am very pleased with the initiative taken by the hon. member for St. John's East, and were the government to introduce such a bill, I would be the first to support it.

speechtext:
Before the committee rose, Mr. Chairman, I was saying that we have now had an opportunity to look at some of the reasons behind this bill.
One of the recent developments is the inquest which has just taken place in Montreal. As one follows the evidence, one appreciates the fact that only the information the prosecutor wishes to bring out is brought out during the proceedings. So the public is still left with an incomplete picture, despite the testimony of Bernard Lortie and Mrs. Rose. Nevertheless, reading the newspaper reports of this testimony one would be hard pressed, in my opinion, to find anything to be particularly scared of, though certain people were exercising a less than normal attitude toward human life in their treatment of individuals.
There is no indication that this was a great conspiracy, or part of a great conspiracy. The inquest proceedings showed that three of those directly concerned were down in Texas with the mother of two of them. They heard about the Cross kidnapping and then drove night and day to get back to Canada. They returned because they felt the others had kidnapped the wrong man, that they had no chance of securing the release of prisoners in accordance, I presume, with an FLQ decision made at a higher than cell level, that nothing could be expected from the kidnapping of Cross, a British diplomat, and that they would have to lay their hands on a political figure from Quebec. So they went out and captured Mr. Laporte.
The evidence at the inquest suggests that these were young people who acted on the spur of the moment, without planning. They took Mr. Laporte to a house where they had food enough for only one day. Indeed, they had to borrow from Mr. Laporte sufficient money for food for the next several days. This does not look like a grand conspiracy to me. It is more like a bunch of punks hell-bent on making a name for themselves in a very bad and nasty way. The testimony indicates that these young people made their decision on the way back. They were very sin-prised at the choice of victim for the other kidnapping, which was also an amateurish job.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? The hon. member said this was decided at the last minute. Did he not read in the report that they had made up their minds, when they were at the Maison des Pecheurs, to kidnap someone?

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
I suppose there were 50 or 75 murders. It is interesting that in Vancouver there are between 25 and 30 murders a year, most of which are not solved. There are many murders in Montreal, I am sure, because of the size of the city. Montreal to many of us is just a city to
visit, but we must not forget that it is a very large city with some two millions inhabitants, and that murder is not unusual there. Four or five attempts, with plans or arrangements, had been made to kidnap other people. I believe the kidnapping of Mr. Laporte was probably more accidental than the evidence at the inquest would lead us to assume. I give some credit to the rumour, and it is only a rumour, that it was the Postmaster General whom they intended to capture and that Mr. Laporte was captured only as a substitute. This makes sense, in terms of some of the things which were said at the inquest. It appears to me to have been a very amateurish job.
There is no doubt that there is a problem with these young people. There is a problem in every country of the world with young people today. But to call this a conspiracy to destroy the whole fabric of our government and society is giving these people more credit than they really deserve. Condemn them all you like for the murder they committed and the kidnapping they arranged. At one time, my leader used the phrase that we were using a sledge-hammer to crack a peanut. The bill before us would be hard to justify on the basis of the evidence which came out at the inquest. This was hardly, it seems, part of a large conspiracy to destroy our democracy. It seems that more consideration was given to what was happening in Quebec City, inside the cabinet, and to its reaction to the situation than was given to the kidnapping and to the operations of the kidnappers.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
For example, the government in Quebec city could have fallen apart. We could not have been too strong in our condemnation of this because it did not have time to gain experience as a government, and since this would have been a calamity that had never befallen a provincial cabinet previously, it could not have been anticipated in any way. The point has been made that it should have been anticipated, and I think this is a good point. We should be prepared for such situations.
The reason the Canadian public has been so shocked at the turn of events is that it believed this sort of thing could only happen in a banana republic; that it could not happen to Canadians. But our experiences on the Saturday and Sunday when Mr. Laporte met his untimely end were almost like a psychedelic trip for the entire Canadian public. Some Liberal members have stated that 98 per cent of the Canadian public supported the government, and I think that is true. This is a matter the broadcasting committee will have to examine and to which a great number of people will have to pay close attention.
I am sure that had the Prime Minister asked for the sort of powers that de Gaulle was given when France has been in serious trouble for years and years, the Liberal Party would have given the powers to him. So would the 78 members from the province of Quebec, without any question at all.

Seventy-four. To be fair to the Prime Minister, he was the only Liberal who had any qualms

November 9, 1970

about applying this sort of measure; he was the only one who said it was a dangerous piece of legislation. Every other Liberal was willing to go along with the government.
We shall have to examine why this happened. Perhaps there should be some curtailment of the freedom of the news media to prevent their producing stories that have no basis in fact. For example, Mr. Chairman, if you cast your mind back to that Saturday night when we were debating the proclamation of the War Measures Act, you will recall that it was reported that three bodies had been found. One was at St. Hubert, one at Dorval or some community north of the city, and a third body on the back seat of a car in a parking lot in downtown Montreal-and all were reported to be the body of Mr. Cross. However, somebody must have spirited those bodies away, or something, because they were not factors in the discussions that followed the next day.
The Minister of Justice must concern himself about the presentation of facts to the public in a way that forced us to adopt such a strong position. Most Canadians are very staid people. We come from the northern hemisphere, the colder part of the continent, and we do not usually react in the same manner as the more hot blooded people in temperate climates. As a nation, we reacted to this situation as a bunch of sheep would react.
I attended recently one of those early November 11 Remembrance Day observances in the town of South Porcupine, and was interested to hear many veterans who had served their country and had spent four or five years in uniform defending the very freedoms for which they had fought. Yet I am sure that most of those people would be in favour of law and order to safeguard their liberties. Recent events have made us for the first time consider just what democracy means to us, what we owe to democracy and what democracy owes to us. No doubt there are limits to freedom. There are also certain rights for which we have fought over hundreds of years, which we should guard very sacredly and should be willing to fight very hard and long to maintain.
I suggest that television had something to do with the recent public alarm. It reminded me of the Orson Welles play which took place years ago at Halloween and caused a public stampede in New York city. People turned on the radio news and were told that Martians had landed and were attacking the city of New York. A number of people were killed. Some had listened only to a bit of the play and had not appreciated that it was a play. Most of the people in the United States listened to the play that night, probably because the program on the other station was so bad. As Members of Parliament we will have to consider recent events impassionately and, in my opinion, without political bias. This is the sort of situation that can be duplicated and could possibly stampede people into taking a position that has not properly been thought out and which might make it impossible for the nation to function as a nation.
One thing that has been clear throughout the whole episode which resulted in the invocation of the War
Public Order Act, 1970
Measures Act and in this bill now before the committee is the total failure of our police forces to operate efficiently. This afternoon I boarded a plane in northern Quebec and overheard several businessmen talking about this question. They were concerned about the police because they were connected with municipal politics. They discussed what might happen in their own communities in view of the inability of the police in Quebec to operate efficiently. For example, I am told there are 51 police forces in greater Montreal, most of which do not talk to each other and jealously guard their territory. In the main they are three or four-man police forces. I suggest that some arrangement will have to be arrived at for making police jurisdictions more national in scope. No policemen can better serve a small community than those who know the area. The trouble is that most of these policemen do not have proper training.
What of our provincial police? I am sure every Member of Parliament was amused and at the same time shocked to hear the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police say in a press interview the other day that all we needed to do to wind up the whole matter was to make one telephone call and then have an emergency cabinet meeting. This reminded me of the first speech made by the commissioner shortly after he was appointed, which he was then told was to be his last speech.

The point I would like to make is that our Canadian police forces have not been properly trained in riot control or in preventing assassinations. Our police forces, particularly the RCMP, spend a lot of their time tackling our national drug problem. They have infiltrated the youth, underground drug market. They have trained their dogs to sniff out marijuana, but very few of their dogs have been trained to sniff out explosives, something with which we will probably be concerned for some time yet.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, it would be dangerous for the House to pass this legislation unamended. If the government was justified at all in proclaiming the War Measures Act, that justification lasted for only the first 24 hours. There is a retroactive provision in this legislation. It is like saying that if you belonged to the Kiwanis five years ago, and we now outlaw the Kiwanis, you could automatically be committed to five years in prison. The idea is frightening.
Freedom is an expensive commodity. It has to be safeguarded. I believe the Minister of Justice will be as glad to listen to the conscience of small minority groups as he is to accept the support of members of his own party. The minister could easily be stampeded into taking action that would cut the essential liberties of the Canadian people, unless it is pointed out to him that there are limitations on the amount of freedom we can forgo until the point is reached when we have lost freedom itself. Therefore, I hope he will consider favourably the amendments proposed, particularly those dealing with the retroactive clause. If he does not, he will find he will not have the support of many people in this House.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have listened carefully throughout this debate and have noted an assumption made by many people that economic problems in the province of Quebec have been responsible for the creation of the FLQ.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: Is that so?

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
I wish the hon. member for Hamilton Wentworth would contain himself at least until I get
[The Deputy Chairman.]
started on my remarks. Economic conditions in parts of Quebec may well have been responsible for some of the motivation behind the FLQ, but there are many other factors that one has to consider in this regard. In a situation such as this we are dealing with fanatical people who are not often motivated by logic, and economic problems are things that give rise to logical motivations. I would not like this particular assumption to go completely unchallenged because we are dealing with an extremely serious matter, something we will have to consider for a long time. As the Minister of Justice indicated earlier, we shall have to deal with permanent legislation along these lines at a future date.
Dealing with the legislation before us, as has been pointed out by various ministers the situation at the present time in Quebec is an unusual one. It is dangerous. It requires special measures, indeed, extreme measures. In my view, the people of Canada support the government both with respect to the invocation of the War Measures Act and the introduction of this legislation. A number of amendments having to do with some of the details of the legislation have been outlined by my colleague, amendments which I support, but nevertheless in general I think the people of Canada quite approve the government's actions. More than that, Mr. Chairman, the people of Canada want terrorists, terrorism and terrorist activities stopped.
Three or four years ago there was a general attitude in this country of allowing people in Canada to do their own thing. This extended to freedom of expression, no matter how free it might be. It was thought people should be allowed to do anything they wished, no matter what violent means accompanied their activities. But after the recent events in Quebec, particularly the horrifying murder of the provincial Minister of Labour, people have had enough of this. There has been a great change of opinion in Canada, a great feeling of revulsion toward this sort of activity. There is no doubt about that.
Some of us try to get around a bit and talk about these matters. We are not entirely confined to the ivory towers in Ottawa. We try to find out what people are thinking. In my view, most people are completely disgusted at the recent actions of this tiny minority group in Quebec, and indeed of related minority groups holding similar ideas in other parts of the country. People wish this kind of thing to be dealt with. I have had a great many letters, as I am sure have all hon. members, on this subject. From the inquiries and observations I have made, I have the impression that about 85 per cent of the people of Canada wish this Parliament to bring in pretty severe measures to deal with activities such as murder, kidnapping for political purposes and threats to blow up airliners with passengers on board, such as the FLQ reportedly has done.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
As I have indicated, a few years ago people were more inclined to be sympathetic toward killers and murderers. They seemed to take the position that perhaps it was not their fault and we should look after them. Now, however,
November 9, 1970

people have come to the conclusion that we cannot go along with that idea entirely and that something must be done about people who, although they may be psychotic, are motivated to do these things. People are beginning to realize there should be some sympathy extended to the victims of murderers rather than to the murderers themselves.
The remarks I shall make in the next moment or so I indended to make at perhaps a later date when more permanent measures are brought in by the Minister of Justice, as promised. On second thoughts, however, it would seem that these remarks might be appropriate at the present time. This bill has a limited life. It is a temporary measure which is to expire next April. In view of the fact that it is a temporary measure, it would seem to me we might as an experiment introduce certain amendments. I would hope the Minister of Justice would give consideration to these.

As my colleague the hon. member for Calgary North has said, the Minister of Justice has not yet indicated what he might agree to. I suppose he is reserving his decision in this regard until he has heard all the representations. I hope this is the case. The present bill is more acceptable to, but reminiscent of, the regulations under the War Measures Act. It would seem to me that since we are in the middle of an experimental period regarding the removal of the death penalty in Canada, except of course in respect of a policeman or other law officer-apparently it is all right if the Governor General or a like person should be killed-the government might be well advised, because of the unusual circumstances which exist in Quebec, which on the government's own admission will probably exist until April, to reinstate the death penalty for murder during this period. In addition to that, since the FLQ reportedly has threatened to carry out bombings and kidnappings and has threatened death to victims, it might be desirable that capial punishment also be introduced as a temporary measure in respect of kidnapping where threats of death are made, or in respect of the hijacking of aircraft involving a threat to blow up the aircraft with passengers on board.
I would think these things might be introduced on a trial basis until next April. I do not wish to become involved in the argument concerning capital punishment versus non-capital punishment. Such arguments have been heard many times. We have heard that capital punishment is not a deterrent. In many cases capital punishment probably is not a deterrent when we are dealing with fanatical people. But very often it is a deterrent. If we were to follow the argument to its logical conclusion, we might ask why it is necessary to have penalties in law if none of them is deterrent. There is no doubt in my mind that capital punishment is a deterrent, and so long as it would prevent people being murdered or blown up I think it would accomplish something.
Public Order Act, 1970
Thinking back to a time when I was very young, I recall a notorious kidnapping. I refer to the kidnapping of the son of Charles Lindbergh, the Atlantic flyer. This case received a good deal of publicity in the media which I do not think was very helpful. There was a rash of kidnappings throughout the United States at the time. Capital punishment was introduced for kidnapping and this put at stop to it right off the bat. In view of the unusual circumstances in Quebec and perhaps in other parts of Canada at the present time, I suggest that as a trial measure we might introduce the death penalty for murder and political kidnapping as well as hijacking of aircraft. Then we could examine the situation in order to determine the result.
In respect of the experiment we are now conducting concerning the removal of the death penalty, which I believe is to be reviewed in 1973, I think the statistics are somewhat misleading and confusing, but at the present time they would seem to indicate that the murder rate has just about doubled in Canada since the death penalty has been removed. It is more pronounced in some parts of the country than in others. This is a worrisome situation. The rate might have increased in any event. However, the fact is that the murder rate has since the death penalty was temporarily suspended.
I do not think there would be any harm in introducing these extremely harsh measures until next April. The government had no qualms about introducing harsh measures in respect of the province of Quebec, and possibly elsewhere, as has been suggested. It is true that since the troops have been around, the FLQ people have been playing doggo. They are lying low. But the moment the troops are gone, their activity may start again. I would hope the minister would consider putting some of these measures into effect until next April. Then if it should appear they have had a beneficial effect, well and good. If not, they can be reviewed. I believe this is a suggestion which should be considered and adopted.

Mr. Chairman, the bill before us is the result of tragic events which happened in Quebec.
It is most unfortunate that this measure was not among the laws already existing and able to deal with the case of the FLQ. Such a law would have been much more suitable to the problem than the War Measures Act which the government had to invoke.
God willing, Mr. Chairman, I hope that we never have to invoke the legislation before us even if it is much less stringent than the War Measures Act.
This provisional bill it intended to replace the War Measures Act in this period of emergency. It is not a permanent bill, and I believe that the government deserves to be commended for dalaying the introduction of a permanent bill at a future date when calm has been completely restored and the judgment of individuals and Parliaments is more detached.

November 9, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
Hon. members opposite strike at details of the events. They desperately seek something on which to hang on to in order to defend untenable positions. They speak about the lack of information, while they already have supported much more stringent legislation with less information, as it were. They speak about the abuse of rights and repression, while they mention no name or no action to prove it. They speak about numerous rumours which allegedly come from sources inside the government, without having the courage to check those rumours and to reveal their authors.
Opposition parties say that they will support this legislation although they will submit amendments. Let us see what is suggested in this legislation.
It is asserted that our freedom is possible only to the extent that it rests on the respect of moral and spiritual values and on the supremacy of the law. I will never believe that one could deny this principle unless one is an anarchist.
It is also stated that the FLQ has exercised violence in Canada and that this movement is still dangerous. Certainly no one will deny that. In fact, that violence goes back to 1963 and continues with increased intensity.
It is stated that the Canadian Parliament wishes to take measures to protect society. Surely we will not be asked to wait for an insurrection before considering necessary legislation. In fact, the New Democratic Party blames the government for invoking the War Measures Act when other legislation was available. What other legislation, Mr. Chairman?
Even if the War Measures Act was secretly proclaimed, 40 odd persons are now being sought and remain undiscoverable.
It is said that the FLQ is an unlawful association. Indeed, all hon. members agree on that. One would have to be extremely naive to believe that the FLQ is a lawful and commendable association.
It is said that if an offence is committed after this legislation is enacted, the past record of an FLQ member could serve as evidence against him. I cannot see that the FLQ members could not be identified as such before the coming into force of the legislation.
Some punishment is recommended for FLQ accomplices or supporters. Surely they are as guilty as those they help.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
It is suggested that detention be much shorter than that stipulated by the War Measures Act. It must be recognized that detention is necessary in such circumstances.
Arrests are to be made without warrant. Of course such a proposal opens the door to abuse. But how can we fight the abuses of a revolutionary movement without adopting very severe measures?
It proposes entering without warrant any premises suspected of harbouring terrorists. Everyone will agree that such premises must be entered in order to find proofs and arrest the terrorists. A similar provision must also apply to the seizure of objects found on those premises.
Finally, the act is to apply for a set period of time. This shows that the government is intent upon avoiding abuse in the application of such severe and serious bills. While recognizing the seriousness of the situation, the government is anxious to normalize it and a definite duration is given to this bill.
I am convinced that the majority of my constituents will approve me when I have the pleasure of supporting Bill C-181.

But I want to put on the record again a couple of paragraphs from the speech the minister made in the House on October 16. It is reported at page 224 of Hansard. Among other things, the minister said on that occasion:
Any person having knowledge of the FLQ organization in the province of Quebec at the present time cannot but be aware that the state of Quebec and the federal state are truly in danger in Canada.
Why? The most pessimists say that the FLQ has some 3,000 members.
An hon. member interrupted and said, "More". The minister continued:
I do not know if that figure is accurate but I am aware that there are quite a few.
And I know something else: these people have infiltrated every strategic place in the province of Quebec, every place where important decisions are taken, and without giving complete details let us say that at the present time they are in a position to cause the Quebec and the federal governments, as well as the city of Montreal, irreparable harm, with the support of outside organizations which are not necessarily in agreement as to the measures taken because it is well organized.
Some say: Why have you not made it illegal? That is what we are doing under these regulations though it might not be the best solution. It is known that the FLQ is made up of cells of two or three persons each, cells that do not know each other, that do not necessarily work hand in hand and that are now in touch simply through coded messages broadcast free of charge by our radio stations.
I pause to make it clear that the minister said that coded instructions were going out over radio stations. He did not imply, as the right hon. member for Prince Albert this afternoon attempted to imply, that those people worked for the CBC. They may have worked for other stations. It is interesting that we have not heard the minister repeat these very serious allegations since October 16. What about those coded instructions that were going out? Have the people involved been apprehended? Have they been charged? What about the infiltration that has been alleged? Were the police of Montreal infiltrated? Were the Quebec provincial police, the Royal Canadi-

an Mounted Police and the armed forces infiltrated? We do not know, Mr. Chairman.

It seems to our members, as it seems to most newspaper reporters, that if these charges were based on facts, we should have been told this so we could deal with it. It is because we have not got any of the evidence which may or may not exist-it has not been given to us or the public-that we have our doubts about the procedures which the government has followed. I ask the Minister of Justice why the government waited until October 15 or 16 to take action. After all, the activities of the FLQ did not begin with the kidnapping of Mr. Cross and Mr. Laporte? Bombings by the FLQ began in 1963, and thefts of dynamite have been going on for years.
What steps did the government take to combat the subversive, illegal actions of the FLQ? Was the security and intelligence section of the RCMP beefed-up between 1963 and 1970? We do not know, Mr. Chairman. The police forces in Canada have not been able to infiltrate the terrorist organizations in Quebec in the same manner as the FBI-without the acts that the government of Canada has asked Parliament to pass-has been able to infiltrate terrorist organizations in the United States. Canadians have a right to know what the government was doing between 1963 and 1970 to eliminate the dangers which have arisen and which occurred previously, namely, the dangerous, illegal, terrorist actions of the FLQ.
I believe that police action is necessary. But that alone will not eliminate the causes which led to the feelings of frustration which produced the terrorists of Quebec. I am not going to discuss economic and social conditions in Quebec, but I suggest that the Minister of Justice should read carefully the statement made last week by the Quebec Welfare Council, which is certainly not a very radical organization, to the Senate Committee on Poverty. They described the kind of situation that exists in the slum areas of Montreal and Quebec, the lack of adequate housing, recreational facilities, medical and hospital services. Until we do something about this situation, we will not eliminate those feelings which permit the FLQ to get the support of a small percentage of the people of the province of Quebec. Until we do that, we will fail.
The people of Canada, especially those in Quebec, are upset, disturbed and frightened because of what has occurred in the province of Quebec during the past few years. It is not surprising they feel the way they do. It would be surprising if they could be objective about the situation. They want action. We support their feelings. We support the government in any action it takes to correct the situation and to apprehend those who are guilty. Some people, including some members of this House, feel that the danger is so great that in order to stamp out the danger it may be necessary to arrest some innocent people; that this is not too great a price to pay. Some have said that you cannot make an omelet without breaking some eggs. Although I understand that feeling, I do not agree with it. We have tried to read and understand history. We have looked at other countries and we

have looked at the attempts of colonial powers to stop independent movements by imprisoning the leaders of those movements. All those attempts met with failure, Mr. Chairman.
I suggest to the Minister of Justice, who has some family relationships in Winnipeg, that he read the history of Winnipeg. In 1919, faced by a strike the government of the day passed an amendment known as section 98 of the Criminal Code which gave that government tremendous powers. Under that section of the Criminal Code they arrested and imprisoned six or more strike leaders. There is no similarity between the leaders of the 1919 strike and the leaders of the FLQ. The leaders of the 1919 strike believed, as we do, that changes in the system can be made democratically. However, Mr. Chairman, they were imprisoned because they led a strike.
The result of imprisoning those men has been that for more than 50 years the people of Winnipeg, at least that part represented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself, in almost every federal and provincial election have elected representatives who are not members of the Liberal party or the Conservative party. The arrests and imprisonment of the strike leaders resulted in a feeling of hostility toward the establishment which still exists among a large group of people in Winnipeg.
I am opposed to the FLQ, their philosophy and methods of terror. I disagree with them completely. Although separatism would be a disaster for the province of Quebec and Canada, advocating separatism by democratic means is not illegal. When people who are not terrorists are arrested and imprisoned, we are creating martyrs and sympathy for the cause of separatism.
I would support this bill if I felt that it gave the government and the police authorities the powers they need, but I cannot support it if it contains provisions which drastically curtail the democratic rights of people, or if it contains provisions which would make its penalties retroactive. That is completely contrary to the basic premise of a democratic system. I urge the government to consider seriously and agree to amendments which will make the bill fair and acceptable to members of this House and all Canadians.

I suggest the following French version of clause 3:
Le groupe de personnes ou 1'association qui s'appelle Front de Liberation du Quebec, ou tout groupe ou association lui succe-dant ainsi que tout groupe ou toute association qui preconise de recourir a la force ou au crime pour realiser au Canada un changement de regime politique identique ou analogue a celui que preconise ledit Front de liberation du Quebec ou pour y contribuer sont declares etre des associations illegales.

Although my English is not very good, I should just like to say I have attempted both in this amendment and in the other amendments, without touching the essence of the provisions, to try to draft a better French version. As hon. members know, the content of this legislation is in fact mainly addressed to French Canadians, and I think the French version is very bad. This is why I have tried to make a better translation, and I hope I have succeeded. At least the French version will be more readable and will not look like a colonial law drafted by the English for the French Canadians, without the French style. What I just read was my amendment, and if I do succeed in changing the wording of the clause in my second amendment it will at least be more readable in French. I will now continue in French to say what to me is bad about clause 3.

It must be noted here that three categories of associations or groups are declared illegal. First, the FLQ; secondly, its successors; thirdly, any other association
which would advocate the use of force or crime to reach the same or substantially the same goal as the FLQ.
It must be noted that this clause is entirely different from the second paragraph of the preamble which is actually restricted to the FLQ. It is my deep conviction, in the first place, that clause 3, beginning at paragraph 5, is ambiguous, or, if you want, can be interpreted in so many different ways that it is totally inconsistent with the usual rules governing the wording of an exceptional law, considering that this legislation is characterized by quite excessive powers which must be counterbalanced by a scope of enforcement as clearly defined and restricted as possible.
I am prepared to believe that the subject matter of this legislation, as stated, is restricted to the FLQ. However, allow me to point out that whoever drafted this legislation has a very poor knowledge of the FLQ movement. What did he mean by:
-the same or substantially the same-
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

-in accomplishing the same or substantially the same governmental change within Canada as that advocated-
-by the FLQ. In Webster's Third International Dictionary, 1967, "substantially" is defined as relating to the main part of something". Then I would ask, what is the main part of the FLQ? Nobody can say what it is. That is why I say the words "or any group" at the end of line 5 give rise to any interpretation.

For instance, the communique No. 11 of the FLQ dated November 2-and it is known today to have been a fake-read in part as follows:
The FLQ does not aim at political power; we are determined to make the revolution, as it is the only way lor the Quebec workers to come into power.
Such stupid and morbidly anarchic nonsense is not even original. It is typical of all movements which keep harping on anarchic concepts termed by Lenin as a passtime for bourgeois.
Finally, it is essential to show that clause 3, as worded, especially paragraph 5, lends itself to unacceptable interpretations in an exceptional legislation. Once more, the good intentions are exemplar: in fact, the circumstances are not deemed favourable to the introduction of a comprehensive bill, but I say that the challenge was not taken up.
Indeed, if one carefully considers the third group to whom the legislation applies, any group whose goal would be "the same or substantially the same"-
Now, let us agree on terms. What is the aim of the FLQ?
I find regrettable that such tremendous powers are given to the police over groups or associations when the wording of clause 3 makes it impossible to determine what is the prevailing element in the FLQ. In this connection, I shall give only one example: If two Newfoundlanders conspire to kidnap a federal minister represent-

November 9, 1970

ing a British Columbia riding, are they pursuing the same or substantially the same goals as those of the FLQ?
Another example: when an hon. member states that violence is spread not only by those we suspect, but also by Messrs. Laberge, Pepin and Claude Ryan, adding in the same breath that such people should be shot ten at a time, without trial, as well as some ten FLQ leaders, is he not pursuing goals very close to those of the FLQ?
Here is another illustration: let us assume that by ill luck a few distraught hot-heads among the Lapalme exemployees were to explode a bomb, and considering that the FLQ had also resorted to criminal acts in order to impose the solution to their problems, would they be pursuing an objective by advocating means fairly similar to that of the FLQ?
In short, it may be seen to what extent the second half of clause 3 may lead to all kinds of interpretations and, again, the person who has been arrested on mere suspicion has no recourse. If it is true that the wording of legislation in general terms is preferable, the situation is altogether different when it comes to a provisional and exceptional measure which provides policemen with practically unlimited powers and eliminates any recourse for the arrested persons.
What does clause 3 actually mean? Briefly, it deals with associations which advocate the same means for accomplishing the same objectives. Obviously, clause 3 thus summarized is not as restricted as mentioned in the preamble.
That is all the more serious as jurisprudence is constant: in case of conflict between the preamble and a section of the act, the latter prevails. The preamble reads as follows:
-within Canada with respect to the Province of Quebec-
-whereas clause 3 stipulates:
-within Canada-
So if a Newfoundlander, member of a secret organization, comes to Ottawa to kidnap a federal minister from British Columbia will he not also be pursuing "substantially the same" goal as the FLQ?
What is the FLQ's goal? I would be pleased if somebody would explain it to us. Violent anarchy? It may be, but the criteria to define it are very nebulous.
I propose a version of clause 3 which is at least French, and fundamentally I propose to delete in line 6 the words:
-that advocates-
-and to substitute therefor
"appointed or described in an order of the Governor General in Council".
Evidently, my proposal does not entirely solve the problem, but it leaves to politicians the task of making decisions which could be discussed. If the bill is passed without amendment, an individual could be arrested and detained without bail. Only after several months, the Court could rule that he belonged to an association which was not unlawful. In my opinion, it is essential that the
Public Order Act, 1970
associations coming under the legislation be clearly identified.
I move that at line 6 which reads in English as follows:

The clause refers to any group of persons or association that is enumerated in a special order. That means at least there could be a debate on the decision of the government to call it an unlawful association. By the other law, an agent of the peace might arrest somebody whose association, in his opinion, was unlawful and it would take months before the courts decided that question. Therefore, I think the "loi exceptionnelle" should be the clearest possible. C'est tout.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member tor New Westminster is perhaps contusing Committee of the Whole with a Standing Committee. In Committee of the Whole there is no rule which requires anyone to give notice of any amendment: we can move amendments as we go from clause to clause. It is impossible to arrange, every time someone moves an amendment, to have it duplicated and made available to all members in writing. I think such a procedure would be completely unworkable for all of us in respect of all bills.
This is not the only bill that has been before Committee of the Whole in this or in other parliaments. There have been bills just as complicated as this one. This is the way in which we have always had to proceed in Committee of the Whole. A little attention as things proceed makes it not too difficult to follow the amendments moved. The hon. member says it is impossible to vote on an amendment on clauses 4 or 5 without realizing its relationship to clauses 9 or 10. Of course, in such a situation it is the duty of the hon. member moving the amendment to indicate, if he knows, what its relationship will be to other clauses of the bill, if there is a relationship, and for other hon. members to agree to it or oppose it, indicating the effect it would have on some other part of the bill. I do not know of any other way it can be done otherwise.
I am under no obligation to give the members of this House copies of the amendments I propose to move. As it happens, we have given copies to the Minister of Justice because he is piloting the legislation through the House and we thought it only fair that he should see those amendments so that he could consider whether or not he agreed with them. But there is no obligation under the rules to do this. There is nothing to stop an amendment being brought to the floor as was done by the hon. member for Regina East earlier this evening. He moved it because he thought of something which ought to be improved. Should we not have voted on it, and should we have held up proceedings until it was duplicated?
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, this is an impossible suggestion, much as I appreciate the desire of the hon. member to have everything in writing before him. He might ask people who move amendments to read them slowly while he writes quickly, but that is about the only solution we could have to that problem.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is always a great thing in one's life to see everybody fleeing as if they were-

speechtext:
-being threatened by the plague, when one gets up to speak on the late show. None the less, I rise in an effort to do my duty. I do it for obvious reasons. The great question which brings us here tonight is the question I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) which may be found by referring to page 876 of Hansard. I am sure everybody has looked at it four or five times in the last hour or so. My question is the following:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance and arises from the speech to the British Columbia Federation of Labour by the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada about employment and unemployment forecasts. Does the government agree with these projections?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I have not seen them at this point. I will take a look at them.
I then posed another question to the minister:
When the minister answers that question, will he also say what the government expects the unemployment situation to be if he differs from the chairman?
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Really, Mr. Speaker, that is the sum and substance of my being here tonight trying to press for an answer to what surely must be the most important question for Canadians at this time. It is not an esoteric question; it does not deal with anything that happens abroad. It deals with what I would call the lunch-pail question: Is somebody going to have work? Will somebody be able to go home to his wife and children with money and say, "This is what I have been able to earn"?
I had to go home in somewhat different circumstances myself when I was faced with certain facts in 1963. But the fact is that every cotton-picking man or bread earner among us has to assume a certain posture. That may mean nothing to the Minister of Finance, but to us it may mean a very important posture-the right to be a
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion man or woman, or the right not to be. It was in the spirit of that sort of question that I asked what was the forecast. The Minister of Finance cast it off in a cavalier fashion over his left shoulder. In that respect he almost becomes an imitative shrugger of his boss, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). But he answered it by saying, in effect: Oh, well; in due course that question would come before us. When I presented the question I did so seriously and I expected a serious answer, and I still do.
I should like to read 143 words into the public record. They come from the report of the Economic Council of Canada. The group of people who presented the report to the Minister of Finance was composed as follows, as appears at page 15 of the annual report of the Economic Council:
The council is assisted by a staff of approximately 120 persons, including about 60 professional and administrative officers, drawn from a wide variety of former positions with the federal government departments, other federal agencies, provincial governments, universities, business firms, labour unions, and international institutions. The wide range of training, experience and knowledge of the staff reflects the wide terms of reference given to the council. In spite of these wide terms of reference, there has been a deliberate attempt to keep the over-all size of staff relatively small and to expand it relatively slowly in order to maintain strength and consistency in the work of the council.
In the spirit of finding strength and consistency I ask the question: Where are we going, employment or unemployment-wise, this winter in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to be precise about the particular rate of growth in the economy that is required to give a given level of employment or unemployment, and the government is not prepared to comment on the projections made by the chairman of the Economic Council.
In his remarks during the Throne Speech debate, the Minister of Finance on October 13 dealt at some length with the present state of the economy, the difficult nature of the problems confronting us and the steps taken by the government thus far to deal with them. It may be recalled that the minister acknowledged, too, the fact that, as he put it, we shall need a substantial annual rate of real growth before any marked improvement in the unemployment rate will be forthcoming. These are the hard facts.
The minister also expressed his confidence that the economy is capable of returning to the rate of growth that will reduce the unemployment rate significantly over the next four or five quarters. He said:
We believe that our policy stand will guide the economy on this course.
The government will do the people of Canada no service if it rekindles the inflation by seeking to force an advance more rapid than productivity improvement and cost moderation will permit.
Before concluding, it may be worth reminding the House that in its last review the Economic Council itself stressed the extreme importance of moving the economy back toward its potential gradually, and with great care, so as to avoid the danger of renewed inflation.

November 9, 1970
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion MANPOWER-SUCCESS OF RETRAINING PROGRAM IN PROVIDING JOBS

maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT-FORECASTS BY ECONOMIC COUNCIL CHAIRMAN-GOVERNMENT REACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 5 I posed a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) asking him to give a statement to the House regarding the effectiveness of the training and retraining program carried out by the department. I wanted to know specifically whether this program was successful, because on the same day in response to a question at page 904 of Hansard the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had said:
Mr. Speaker, as I have pointed out before, the winter works program totalled something less than $50 million. We have replaced it by manpower retraining and mobility programs to the tune of several hundreds of millions of dollars.
The Prime Minister was boasting about this, saying this is the type of thing the government was doing in order to alleviate the unemployment situation. But I simply want to know how effective is the program. I do not see the minister nor the Parliamentary Secretary here, but I am sure somebody will answer the question. This important question lies at the heart of the problem in order to deal with unemployment and poverty in Canada.
To my knowledge we have not had a real accounting of the effectiveness of the program. I do not wish to criticize the program out of hand or disregard its benefits, but I am concerned that the government seems to place practically all its efforts to deal with unemployment on this manpower retraining program, and I submit that it does not always work though a great deal of money is spent. Last year the government issued press releases about the amount of money spent, but there was no mention of its effectiveness in bringing people from these courses into the labour force.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT-FORECASTS BY ECONOMIC COUNCIL CHAIRMAN-GOVERNMENT REACTION
speechtext: There were no jobs to go to.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT-FORECASTS BY ECONOMIC COUNCIL CHAIRMAN-GOVERNMENT REACTION
speechtext:
That is exactly the problem-there are no jobs. This is why I want to know how the program is being assessed. It is better to have a program than to simply pay unemployment insurance. At least it gives the trainees something to do, but in itself that is not good enough.
What relation is there between the training and the unemployment situation? If we have 1,000 people or 1,000 jobs, are the 1,000 people trained for the 1,000 jobs, or is it the other way around? If we have 1,000 people training for particular jobs, are the same 1,000 people being employed in the field that they have chosen? How do we assess the program? Is it by the employment or is it simply by the training that we give?
For example, I am aware of a program where 700 people applied but only 200 were accepted. This raises the question of whether it is a program for the elite, if I may use that term in this context. Naturally, the best people get the training but what happens to the other 500 who applied for training under this program? Do we send them to other courses? I do not know the answer and this is why I asked for a statement, because if we have to shift people to other courses it presents another problem.

[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Are we simply trying to offer a complete range of courses? That is a question I should like answered. For example, I know of one case in which a gentleman was told to apply for three or four courses. That does not make much sense. Either he is suited for one course or he is not. Perhaps he did not want to take three or four courses; he only wanted one course. The department did not want him to apply for only one course. Apparently they did not have that course to offer. Why do they not tell the applicant they do not have the course, and try to help him in some other way? Let us not shift these poor people around.
Many questions could be asked about this training program. I want to know how the government assesses it. After going through a training program, are the people suitable for employment? Also, is the government really providing incentives for employers to hire these people? The first thing an employer asks an employee is, "Have you had any experience?" We must do something to encourage employers to hire these people. For all these reasons I want to know how effective is this program.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT-FORECASTS BY ECONOMIC COUNCIL CHAIRMAN-GOVERNMENT REACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member's receptiveness to enlightenment will be commensurate with his ingenuity for framing questions. In replying to the hon. member's question, I would say first that for the fiscal year 1969-70 alone some 320,000 persons were placed in training under the Canada Manpower Training Program. With reference to the success of this program, I would refer him to a survey tabled by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration on June 22, 1970, on adults who have taken Canada Manpower training courses. This survey involved 83,193 persons who completed full-time courses in public institutions between January and September 30, 1969, and indicates that graduates of Canada Manpower training courses have more than doubled their prospects of getting a job and increased their earnings potential by at least 12 per cent.
As these figures indicate, the results of this survey are very encouraging and demonstrate that the Canada Manpower training courses make a very positive contribution to higher productivity and income security for Canadian families. Specifically, the survey shows that 75 per cent of those who finished training and looked for work were fully employed within three to four months. Only 31 per cent were employed when they entered courses. Men increased their average earnings by $43 a month, and women by $47 a month. This was a gain of 11 per cent over pre-training earnings for men, and 24 per cent for women. Seventy-one per cent of those who took skill training found jobs in occupations closely related to their training.
I would also point out that this survey forms but part of the Department of Manpower and Immigration's continuing review and evaluation of the effectiveness of the training programs for adults. This review and evaluation is believed to be the most comprehensive of any country's. With reference to the higher proportionate wage gains for women, I would mention that one of the great
November 9, 1970

virtues of the training program is that it is tending to equalize opportunity for women who prior to training had substantially lower earnings. This is true for both women taking skill courses and those in basic upgrading.
These results indicate that, particularly in the case of women, improvement in the basics alone can lead workers to a more rewarding job and bring about a substantial increase in productivity and earnings. None the less, trainees who go to further skill development can, judging from the results, expect an additional increase in earnings. Both men and women completing skill courses showed substantially higher earnings after training than those taking upgrading courses.

maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-CORNWALL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON STUDIES AND PROGRAMS
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-CORNWALL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON STUDIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 29, as reported at page 693 of Hansard, I directed the following question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand):
Will the minister give consideration to making a statement on motions outlining the results of studies made by the federal government and the government of Ontario into the heavy unemployment in the Cornwall area and an early start on various programs under the provisions of the DREA legislation?
My question was prompted by the continuing concern of many people about the situation in the Cornwall area. In December of last year the secretary of the textile workers' union in Cornwall wrote to the minister, I think, and to the leader of the NDP pointing out that 650 people had been given notice of permanent lay-off by the Cour-taulds plant in Cornwall.
On April 13 of this year the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) directed a question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, pointing out that in the area of Stormont-Dundas-Glengarry 13.7 per cent of the total labour force was unemployed. He asked what was being done. The minister replied that his deputy had visited Cornwall and they would be giving serious consideration to the question.
On May 25, 1970, the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Douglas) directed a question to the same minister pointing out that the unemployment rate in Cornwall was approximately 18 per cent. He asked what the results, if any, had been of the special task force studying the situation in the Cornwall area, whether a report had been received and what action would be
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion taken. On that day the minister said that the task force had returned the week before, that he had not received a recent report but that he would inquire and inform the House of the results of the study within a few days. That was on May 25. It is now November.
If the task force made a report, it is still in the files of the minister. If the task force recommended any special measures to help establish new industries in the Cornwall area, nothing has been done about them to our knowledge. The minister replied to the leader of the New Democratic Party that he had inquired about the plight of the 650 people laid off at the Courtaulds plant and that they had been offered the opportunity of a retraining course. No one wants to downgrade the importance of retraining courses, but it is a rather desperate situation if that is all that can be offered to people in an area such as Cornwall.
If the result of the retraining is that they will be offered jobs in other cities, requiring them and their families to move, this is a very serious situation for the people concerned. I join the right hon. member for Prince Albert, the leader of my party and others in asking the government what steps are being taken to help alleviate the situation in eastern Ontario, particularly in the city of Cornwall.

speakeroldname: Mr. Martin P. O'Connell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-CORNWALL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON STUDIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
For some months, Mr. Speaker, the federal government and the government of the province of Ontario have been working together to develop increased employment in the area of Cornwall. This effort applies not only to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion but to other federal departments such as transport, public works and manpower and immigration, which can help in making Cornwall more attractive to industry. There is a parallel and co-ordinated effort on the part of the various departments of the provincial government.
While I do not have concrete results that can be announced tonight, there is a likelihood that some positive results will occur quite soon. Everyone regrets that the problem is so difficult and solutions take time to develop. Every practical effort to bring them into being as soon as possible is being made.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.23 p.m.
